chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, and from his father, all from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man asked him: 'Do you see that if I see something in the hand of a man, is it permissible for me to testify that it belongs to him?' He said: 'Yes.' The man said: 'I testify that it is in his hand, and I do not testify that it belongs to him, for perhaps it belongs to someone else.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Then is buying from him permissible?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Perhaps it belongs to someone else, so from where did it become permissible for you to buy it and it becomes your property, then you say after acquiring ownership that it is for me, and you swear an oath on it, while it is not permissible to attribute it to the one from whom its ownership came to you?' Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If this were not permissible, the market for the Muslims would not stand.'
ai.seo_question: What is the juristic ruling on testifying to possession versus ownership in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the jurisprudential principle that possession (qabd) serves as the primary evidence for ownership in commercial transactions, allowing buyers to rely on visible possession without needing absolute proof of title. He highlights the logical inconsistency of testifying merely to possession while later swearing absolute ownership, a nuance that ensures the fluidity and trust required for Islamic markets (suq) to function effectively. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on practical legal presumptions (zann) in daily trade, balancing evidentiary rigor with commercial necessity.
